extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and number theorists (and programmers) who use PARI/GP as a programmable calculator or as a library; developers embedding or extending PARI
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for using PARI/GP either interactively (GP calculator) or as a library from higher-level languages; covers data types, operation semantics, defaults/configuration, portability and programming advice for producing correct and efficient PARI code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of use
rubrics_metrics.description: PARI can be used (1) as a library called from an upper-level language (C, C++, Pascal, Fortran) or (2) as a programmable calculator named GP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose library mode for embedding into applications; choose GP for interactive or scripting work. Chapters 2 and 3 explain GP usage; chapters 3–5 explain library programming. A tutorial (tutorial.dvi) is recommended as a first read.

rubrics_metrics.name: PARI philosophy: exactness and permissiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Operations and functions should first give as exact a result as possible, and secondly be permitted if they make any kind of sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you operate on exact objects (non-imprecise), the result will be exact (e.g. 4/3 yields the rational (4/3)). Operations involving imprecise objects produce results 'as precise as possible' and PARI automatically determines correct precision. PARI is permissive: many functions are extended componentwise (e.g. applying exp to a vector yields componentwise exponentials). For situations where componentwise is ambiguous (square matrices), special functions exist (e.g. matexp).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types and recursiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: PARI types are recursive: complex, polynomials, vectors, matrices, lists, etc. are built from basic scalar types (t_INT, t_REAL, t_INTMOD, t_FRAC, t_FRACN, t_COMPLEX, t_PADIC, t_QUAD, t_POLMOD, ...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Components of recursive types can be of different compatible types; for example a complex number a+bi may have a integer and b rational. Beware of creating pathological nested types (e.g. complex-of-complex) — PARI may produce nonsense. Polynomials in several variables are implemented as polynomials with polynomial coefficients. See section 1.2 for full list and discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type compatibility rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Components can be mixed only when types are compatible for the intended operations (e.g., if real is present, integermod components are not allowed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compatibility is defined by whether operations like + or × make sense; mixing incompatible component types can lead to errors or nonsensical results. When designing data structures, prefer homogeneous scalar choices or ensure compatibility across operations you will perform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact vs imprecise objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects containing real, p-adic, or power series types anywhere in their tree are imprecise; other objects are exact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exact objects avoid numerical analysis and are preferable when exact arithmetic is required. Imprecise objects carry precision/approximation metadata and arithmetic on them yields results with computed precision. Understand which parts of your computations are exact vs imprecise to avoid precision-related surprises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and handling of zero for imprecise types
rubrics_metrics.description: For imprecise types zeros are represented with order notation: p-adic zeros are O(p^e), power series zeros O(X^e), real zeros O(2^e)—there are infinitely many distinct imprecise zeros.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precision parameters (like the mantissa precision k) are irrelevant for the identity of a zero; for p-adics and series the exponent e indicates valuation/order. Be careful: small reals or results smaller than the working exponent may be treated as exact zeros in printed output or in further computations (example: 0.E-28 + 1.E-100 yields 0.E-28).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and performance tradeoffs (implementation notes)
rubrics_metrics.description: PARI has multiple implementation variants: assembly-optimized kernels for some architectures (fastest), mixed C/assembly kernels, and a pure-C portable version (slower). PARI is optimized for numbers with at most a few thousand decimal digits; fancy multiplication algorithms beyond Karatsuba are not implemented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a build appropriate to your architecture for best performance. Expect speedups of 5–100× over other CAS on many tasks. For extremely large-digit computations (e.g. 10^7 digits) specialized programs may be better than PARI. See Appendix A for compilation/installation and Appendix C for example functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operation semantics: division and integer/polynomial operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Division is exact when possible (e.g. 4/3 gives rational (4/3)). Integer/polynomial Euclidean division and remainder operators exist (\, %, \/ for quotient with minimal remainder). Exponentiation ^ is defined when exponent is integer; otherwise treated as transcendental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate operators for exact arithmetic; to force real arithmetic use 1./3 or add 0. to an expression. Be aware of operator semantics when mixing types to avoid unintended transcendental evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcendental and componentwise functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Transcendental functions usually operate on any object in C and some on p-adics; by extension PARI applies transcendental functions componentwise to vectors and matrices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This permissive extension is convenient but be explicit if you need matrix-level transcendental operations (use dedicated functions like matexp when implemented). Check Chapter 3 for specific function behaviors and p-adic support.

rubrics_metrics.name: GP metacommands and interactive conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Commands starting with \ or symbols like ? or # are metacommands (non-computational) for interacting with GP — e.g. ? for help, ?functionname for short help, ?? for extended help, ?\ for metacommand list. Ctrl-C interrupts current computation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ?n to see category n (maps to manual Section 3.n). Use ?? or ??? for full descriptions if extended help is available. Metacommands include settings, file operations, history control; see Section 2.2 for keyboard shortcuts and metacommands. Keep Ctrl-C in mind to abort long computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defaults, configuration and string expansions
rubrics_metrics.description: GP has many internal defaults (set via default(def,value)) for behavior: prompt, buffersize, colors, compatible, debug levels, echo, format, help program, histsize, etc. String-valued defaults support time expansion (strftime) and environment expansion ($VAR, ~).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use default(...) to set persistent behavior or put settings in gprc preferences file. String context expansion allows runtime values (e.g. default(logfile, "name" a ".log")). When setting colors or other terminal-related defaults, be aware of terminal/Emacs/readline compatibility issues. See Section 2.1 and misc/gprc.dft for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backward compatibility modes
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'compatible' default controls backward compatibility between GP versions: 0=no compatibility, 1=warn on obsolete functions but accept them, 2=use old naming scheme (case-sensitive differences), 3=attempt to mimic former behavior exactly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer compatible=0 for up-to-date behavior; switching between groups {0,1} and {2,3} can erase previously defined user functions/aliases (variables unaffected). Use whatnow to discover mapping of old functions to new ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting and precision defaults
rubrics_metrics.description: format default controls printed format for reals (xm.n where x in {e,f,g}); the real precision and seriesprecision defaults control internal working precision for real and series arithmetic; buffersize and histsize set buffer and history capacities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set format to suit display preferences (g0.28 default for 32-bit). To print full precision use negative n in format. Adjust realprecision/seriesprecision for desired numerical accuracy; be mindful that combining imprecise operands discards lesser precision digits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portability and OS-specific features
rubrics_metrics.description: Some features (readline editing, extended help, UNIX goodies, EMX ports) depend on build options and OS support. GP includes UNIX- and EMACS-specific conveniences where available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you rely on line-editing or extended help, ensure PARI was compiled with the necessary options and libraries. On non-UNIX systems, some features may be absent or only available via ports (EMX, Cygwin). Consult Appendix A for installation and Appendix file notes for OS-specific behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care with imprecise arithmetic and cancellation
rubrics_metrics.description: When combining imprecise numbers, the resulting accuracy depends on operand precisions, sizes (exponents), and cancellation (size of x+y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unexpected loss of precision or zeros can occur (example: 0.E-28 + 1.E-100 yields 0.E-28). Understand exponent/precision interactions; if you need decimal/real answers from rationals use explicit real forms (1./3) or increase precision. PARI computes result precision automatically, but you must design computations to avoid catastrophic cancellation.
